title: The voices, looking back
tomorrow: how many times does the Lord's Prayer say "I"?

lines: A CHILD OVER A GARDEN WALL.
cards: Advice season. A quote on a mug, a quote in a card, a quote from every relative at once, each pointing a different way. Augustine got his from over a garden wall.
He's in tears under a fig tree when, from a house nearby, a child's voice, he can't tell if it's a boy or a girl, chants over and over: take up and read.

He picks up Paul's letters and reads the first passage his eyes fall on. In his Confessions he says that by the end of that sentence, the darkness of doubt was gone. One voice, from a child he never met.

teach.b: This path has listened to a lot of voices like that one, each speaking from its own road.
Julian of Norwich wrote down what she was shown of God's love, and one line has traveled far beyond her walls: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well."
Teresa of Avila pictured the soul as a castle with many rooms, and prayer as friendship with God.
John Bunyan told of a pilgrim named Christian, bent under a heavy burden, until he reaches the cross and the burden loosens from his back and rolls away.
Thérèse of Lisieux called hers the little way: small things done with great love, when big deeds weren't hers to do. Different times, different churches, very different lives.
None of them wrote with you in mind, and still the words keep arriving, the way a child's chant arrived over a wall. So here's what a voice from the tradition does, and what it doesn't.
It doesn't walk your road for you, and it doesn't make your choice. It lights a stretch of the road so you can see your next step.

how: Some Christians keep a few lines from writers like Augustine, Julian of Norwich, Teresa of Avila, John Bunyan and Thérèse of Lisieux close at hand, reading them slowly in prayer or in reading groups.

o: the angels' songs heard by the shepherds
the opinions of strangers that you should ignore
lines from people of faith that light your own road

s: Augustine heard 'take up and read' from a preacher in church
a child's voice from a nearby house, while he wept in a garden (Confessions 8.12).
Julian's 'all shall be well' comes from her own writing about what she was shown
Thérèse's little way meant doing nothing much at all
small things, done with great love.

games.q: you're Augustine, in tears under a fig tree. a child's voice from next door chants: take up and read. what do you do?
o: go next door to find the child.
ignore it: just a game children play.
pick up Paul's letters and read the first passage you see.
games.why: he took up the book he'd left nearby, Paul's letters, read, and says the darkness of doubt was gone by the end of the sentence.

practice: Choose one line from these voices: take up and read, all shall be well, or a burden rolling away.
Close your eyes and let it come back to you slowly, a few times, as if it had been written to you this morning, and keep it company until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The voices. Augustine, Julian, Teresa, Bunyan, Thérèse: people on their own roads whose words keep arriving on yours.

orig.note: Latin: take up and read, the child's chant Augustine heard in the garden.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: their words, your road; they light a stretch of it, and the walking is yours. That's the day.
